title: The Data Manifold under the Microscope
claim: A small seed dataset is expanded into dense regular grids, from which finite differences yield geometric measures for validating theory.
layout: 3 stages, left-to-right, thick arrow and gear icon linking boxes
description: A left-to-right three-stage pipeline in a wide strip. On the left, a box labeled 'Original Dataset' holds a database cylinder icon and a sparse blue dotted bell-shaped curve. A thick black arrow labeled 'Dataset Expansion' leads to a large central box titled 'Granular Datasets Versions'. It shows dense green point grids over a 3D Gaussian-bump surface, a 1D bell curve, and a polar-grid disc, with larger blue dots marking the original coarse samples. To the right, text reads 'Compute Manifold Measures via finite differences' above a black gears icon. A column of three small surface thumbnails follows, labeled Volume, Reach and an ellipsis, colored in purple and yellow-green gradients. The eye goes first to the central green 3D surface.
caption: From a low-dimensional seed we produce dense, regular grids via analytic parametrizations or systematic transforms; central finite differences recover geometric estimators such as reach and curvature enabling validation of manifold-fitting bounds.
abstract: A significant gap exists between theory and practice in deep learning. Generalization and approximation error bounds are often derived for simplified models or are too loose to be informative. Many rely on the manifold hypothesis and on geometric regularity such as intrinsic dimension, curvature, and reach. Progress requires insight into data-manifold geometry and suitable benchmarks, yet existing options are polarized: analytic manifolds with known geometry but limited applicability, or real-world datasets where geometry is only coarsely estimable. We introduce a benchmarking framework for studying data geometry. We repurpose and extend dSprites and COIL-20 with additional transformation dimensions and dense, axis-aligned sampling, and pair them with finite-difference estimators that recover curvature, reach, and volume at near-ground-truth accuracy in a regime where general-purpose estimators are unreliable or difficult to deploy. The framework is intended as a controlled testbed, useful as a calibration environment for geometric estimators and a sandbox for probing theoretical assumptions. To illustrate its use, we present two application studies, namely assessing the scaling behavior of the bounds of Genovese et al. and Fefferman et al., and tracking the layer-wise geometry of a $Î²$-VAE, highlighting the behavior of current bounds and the value of controlled benchmarks for guiding and validating future theory. A reference implementation is available at https://github.com/koulakis/manifold-microscope.
